title: David B. Wilkins on KPMG's expansion of legal services
author: David B. Wilkins

dom.t: Big Four: Integration matters more than replacement

st.t: Big Four: Integration matters more than replacement
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s central framing: it predicts Big Four strength in selected services integrating law, project management and technology, rather than wholesale displacement of traditional law firms. Its Arizona expansion report also aligns with the cluster’s account of selective regulatory openings, though it provides no evidence of superior delivery or market dominance.
qs: He told Reuters, “‘The Big Four are going to be very good at providing certain kinds of legal services that the traditional law firms have typically in the U.S.
had a monopoly on,’ such as integrating law, project management and technology.”

kp.k: KPMG plans United States legal-services expansion
kp.d: The document reports that KPMG, one of the Big Four accounting firms, plans to expand into United States legal services by opening an office in Arizona. It identifies Arizona’s comparatively open framework for non-lawyer ownership as the regulatory condition enabling this market entry.
qs: KPMG, the Big Four accounting firm, announced its plans to expand legal services in the United States; they plan to open an office in Arizona, which has a more open regulatory framework for non-lawyer ownership of legal services.

kp.k: Big Four may challenge traditional firms’ service monopoly
kp.d: David B. Wilkins predicts that the Big Four will be effective providers of certain services historically dominated by traditional United States law firms. He specifically attributes their potential advantage to combining legal work with project management and technology; the document supplies his expert assessment but no empirical performance evidence.
qs: ‘The Big Four are going to be very good at providing certain kinds of legal services that the traditional law firms have typically in the U.S. had a monopoly on,’ such as integrating law, project management and technology.

kp.k: KPMG is pursuing a tech-enabled multidisciplinary model
kp.d: After the Arizona Supreme Court preliminarily approved KPMG, Wilkins characterized the move as the continuation of a strategy pursued for at least a decade. In his account, KPMG’s model has evolved from imitating law firms at greater scale toward multidisciplinary, technology-enabled service delivery.
qs: After Arizona’s Supreme Court preliminarily granted approval to KPMG, Professor Wilkins told Bloomberg: “This is a natural extension of what they’ve been trying to do for the past decade or more…They went from trying to be like law firms but bigger to pushing a multidisciplinary model that is tech-enabled.”

pts.k: Wilkins predicts Big Four strength in multidisciplinary, technology-enabled legal services; the document makes no explicit AI-specific claim.
pts.d: David B. Wilkins predicts that the Big Four will be effective in certain legal services combining law, project management and technology, areas he describes as traditionally monopolised by US law firms. He characterises KPMG's expansion as a continuation of a shift from imitating larger law firms to a technology-enabled multidisciplinary model. The source does not identify AI as the technology involved or claim AI-driven automation, displacement or productivity gains.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The prediction rests on Wilkins's expert interpretation, contextualised by KPMG's announced expansion and preliminary regulatory approval.
pts.d: The document identifies Wilkins as faculty director of the HLS Center on the Legal Profession and reproduces his comments to Reuters and Bloomberg Law. It reports KPMG's plans for an Arizona office and preliminary approval by Arizona's Supreme Court. These developments provide context for the prediction, not measured evidence of service quality or competitive success. No data, benchmarks or AI performance evidence are supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The expansion is prospective in the 2025 report, while the strategic shift is described as developing over a decade or more.
pts.d: Wilkins gives no deadline for the Big Four's predicted success. His prediction is qualified to 'certain kinds' of legal services rather than the entire market. He places KPMG's move within a decade-plus strategic trajectory. Arizona's openness to nonlawyer ownership and preliminary approval are the stated regulatory context for the planned office, not evidence that comparable entry is permitted throughout the United States.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The identified competitive change concerns Big Four legal-service providers and traditional US law firms.
pts.d: KPMG is the specific entrant, while Wilkins extends his prediction to the Big Four generally. Traditional US law firms face prospective competition in services integrating legal work, project management and technology. The document does not specify effects on particular client groups, lawyer employment, fees or access to justice.
